cells.tense: Right now the questions come easily in shared rooms and land well.
cells.act: set a boundary and hold it
cells.ask: Ask something in a group you belong to and stay with it until two answers disagree before you move on. Keeping it open that long is the boundary.
cells.core:
In rooms where a group keeps something going together — the way it runs a meeting, the story it tells about itself — your questions are working. You ask, people answer, and something gets clearer for the group. This is a gift that hasn't been squeezed into a role yet, and it's doing its job: you hear what someone actually means, ask the next thing, and the conversation moves.

What that could use now is a bit of structure. When you ask, hold the question open a beat longer than is comfortable, long enough for a second voice to disagree with the first. That's the boundary: the question doesn't get folded into the fastest answer. Pick one shared thing this week and try it there. You'll get a truer picture of what the group actually knows, and the asking, which is the part you shine at, gets to keep being yours.
cells.sheetLine: The questions land here, and the group is better for them.
cells.verb: asking a real question into what a group already holds
cells.place: in what a group carries forward together, its rituals and its way of doing things

cells.tense: You're bracing for questions you'll fire into a group before anyone's ready to answer.
cells.act: explore a direction before it has a destination
cells.ask: Take a direction for a group you belong to and go three steps in with no plan — read, ask one person, try it once — then stop and see if the interest is real.
cells.core:
In what your groups carry together, the questions have started sprinting past the room. You're three steps into an inquiry before anyone has heard the first one, and the group keeps having to catch up. The hunger to understand is right; the speed is what's off. You're testing the water by diving.

Let the exploring be real without needing to know where it lands. Pick one direction — a practice, a question, a way of doing something together — and take three steps in, with no destination attached. Read, ask one person, try it once. If it's alive, it will pull you further; if it isn't, you've spent a week, not a group's trust. The point is to feel whether the curiosity is genuine rather than to prove it's right, and the group gets to breathe while you find out.
cells.sheetLine: The questions are outrunning the group again. Take three steps, then stop.
cells.verb: asking a real question into what a group already holds
cells.place: in what a group carries forward together, its rituals and its way of doing things

cells.tense: You used to ask, and the questions no longer arrive in the shared rooms.
cells.act: sense what has not happened yet, with wonder
cells.ask: Give five quiet minutes to sensing what one group you're part of could be in a year if things went well — no notes, no announcement — then leave it be.
cells.core:
You've gone quiet in what your groups pass on. You're present, the rituals still run, but the questions that used to come — the ones that turned a thing over just to see what was inside — don't arrive anymore. The door to that is behind you now, and the close attention you're good at has nowhere to land.

Don't try to force the asking back. Start smaller, with wonder instead: let yourself imagine, once, what one group you're part of could become if a year went well. Five minutes, no notes, nobody told. That act doesn't need the old enthusiasm, only a little space in you that isn't filled with keeping up. If something lifts, the next question will find you without being called. If nothing does, you've lost five minutes and learned where you stand.

It's an offer, not a repair.

cells.tense: The person keeping the room fair is you, and you'd call it just being decent.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: Decide quietly, before you move or speak the next time a group gets under your skin, what would actually be fair here — then carry that call into whatever you do.
cells.core:
In the shared things you're part of, someone keeps them fair. When a comment lands badly, when a meeting leaves one person carrying more than their share, when something goes unsaid too long — the adjustment appears, small and smooth, and the group stays livable. Ask who does it and you'd hear that's just how it is here.

That someone is you, and calling it decency is a way of not signing it. Next time something rubs in a group, pause before you smooth it and name to yourself what would be fair — one sentence you could say aloud. Then say it, or hold it; both count. Knowing the judging is yours is the whole difference. The fairness doesn't start working differently. You just stop being a stranger to your own part in it.

attempts.check: The draft keeps wanting to say the person has *lost* their curiosity, or that a group *taught* them to stop asking — the record supports neither a history nor a cause, only that questions aren't landing in shared settings now. A reader could rightly say 'I ask plenty at work' or 'my doubt is the group's fault' and the cells say nothing of the kind, deliberately; Too Little names a door already stepped through, not who closed it. The asks survive being wrong: each is a small outward act (a real question, a small start, a felt sense of what's next, a clearer word with someone) that teaches something and costs nothing if the read misses. The sentence I cut, because it served me more than them: 'Somewhere along the way you stopped asking, and the room stopped expecting you to' — consequences dressed as cause.
